newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central Africa and army mutineers agree truce.
newsitem.headline: Central Africa and army mutineers agree truce.

text.p: The government of the Central African Republic and army mutineers agreed a 15-day truce on Sunday after mediation by African heads of state to halt a slide into ethnic bloodshed, a spokesman for the mutineers said.
The deal was signed during lengthy talks at the French embassy and the French ambassador's residence in the capital Bangui, the spokesman told Reuters.
The presidents of Gabon, Burkina Faso, Mali and Chad, mandated by last week's Franco-African summit, began meeting the mutineers and other parties to the conflict on Saturday.

The spokesman said under the deal, Mali's former military leader General Amadou Toumani Toure, one of a handful of African leaders to hand over power voluntarily, would examine the causes of the crisis.

The revolt, the third of the year in the impoverished former French colony, began on November 16 over pay demands and an attempt by President Ange-Felix Patasse to redeploy soldiers involved in a May revolt.
It has turned into an attempt to force Patasse, a civilian who was elected in 1993, to step down. Mutineers, who first revolted over pay in April, control parts of Bangui.
Troops from former colonial power France, which intervened in May to keep Patasse in power during a second mutiny, guard strategic points in Bangui with presidential guard and army loyalists.

The spokesman for the mutineers, who put the death toll on all sides at 150 since the latest mutiny began, said Sunday's talks began at 11 a.m. and lasted late into the afternoon. France's ambassador sat in.

Captain Anicet Saulett, leader of the mutineers, told Reuters before Sunday's talks the resignation of Patasse and the departure of what mutineers say are Chadian and Sudanese mercenaries in his pay were non-negotiable.
Burkina Faso's president, Blaise Compaore, left for home before Sunday's talks started.
Bangui residents have reported a spate of tribal killings and abductions pitting southern Yakomas who dominate the rebel ranks against Patasse's northern Bayas.
Precise numbers have proved difficult to verify but victims include former interior minister Christophe Grelombe, a Yakoma, and his son, who were seized on Thursday and murdered.

Eleven opposition parties have signed a memorandum blaming Patasse for the turmoil and accusing him of ignoring accords that ended the May mutiny. "He is no longer in a position to embody national unity," they said.

Gabon's president, Omar Bongo, said after meeting Patasse on Saturday that Africans had to sort out the crisis. "The Central African Republic must not become another Rwanda, a Somalia, a Liberia or a Sierra Leone," he told French radio.
Bangui remained tense but calm on Sunday following isolated overnight gunshots. Markets stayed closed.
France has expressed support for the elected government but President Jacques Chirac said its troops based in the country under defence pacts would not help it combat the mutineers.
"French troops may only take part in maintaining order to avoid major abuses and protect foreign communities," he told reporters after the Franco-African summit in Burkina Faso.
